source_quality.notes: text layer covers all 18 pages; figures read from the text around them

task_reconstruction: Fit water access with a two-predictor line and then an eight-predictor one, forecast India to 2031 with a climate correction, and test two interventions.

section_map.summary: summary of the two models, the forecast and the policy
the need, the drivers and the case of India
the eight-predictor model chosen from twenty
the test on India and the forecast to 2031
the test of the two chosen policies
the conclusions and the future work

contributions.summary: a two-predictor baseline explaining 43.7 percent of the variance
an eight-predictor model, chosen from twenty, explaining 71.6 percent
a climate correction that lowers the 2031 forecast by 2.68 points
two policies that together more than offset the climate loss

dependency_graph.relation: the simple fit is the baseline the refined one is measured against
the forecast access is what the yearly loss is subtracted from
the drop in population growth changes one predictor

assumptions.summary: predictors are linear and uncorrelated, and the data and errors are normal
access to water is an inverse proxy for scarcity
the fitted relationships hold for fifteen years
population growth proxies for demand and income per person for the ability to meet it
water supply stays at its recent average apart from the climate loss

data_and_preprocessing.summary: 147 countries and twenty candidate predictors cut to eight
missing 2012 air pollution filled by the mean of 2011 and 2013
each predictor projected from its own previous ten years

models.summary: two-predictor line of access on income and growth
eight-predictor line chosen by a best-subset search
a linear climate correction from a published projection
population growth fitted on women's secondary enrollment

verification.summary: the fit rerun with India removed, moving the prediction by one point
the 2012 prediction set against the published 92.2 percent
the forecast crossed four ways with the policies and the climate

results_trace.summary: access rises from 84.2 percent in 2012 to 94.4 percent in 2031
the climate correction brings 2031 down to 91.7 percent
both policies with the climate correction give 95.9 percent against 92.1

writing_logic.summary: the summary opens on a borrowed line before any number
the simple model is kept so the refined one can beat it
the rising forecast is set against warnings of a crisis
the close separates rough levels from clear trends

language_observations.summary: opens by quoting the Ancient Mariner
reads a slope as a one-unit change, everything else held constant
owns a positive slope where a negative one was expected
trusts the ranking of the effects and not the exact level

visualization_observations.summary: Figure 1 plots the two predictors of the baseline
Table 2 gives the coefficient and the p-value of each kept predictor
Table 5 crosses the policies with the climate correction
Figures 4 and 5 draw access over time with and without the policies

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: keeping the weak model as a baseline makes the refinement readable as a gain
reporting the wrong-way sign instead of dropping it reads as honest

weaknesses.summary: the air pollution slope has the wrong sign and is kept
the forecast rises where other work warns of a crisis
two predictors are proxies for quantities never observed
the enrollment fit explains little of the growth

independent_extensions.summary: cut a long predictor list to the subset with the best adjusted fit and report the lift
refit with the case country removed to see whether it props the model up

unresolved_questions: the autoregression that projects each predictor is described but never written out
the air pollution slope is positive against expectation and no refit drops it
the eight-point gap between the 2012 prediction and the published figure is never closed
a loss of water supply is treated as an equal loss of access
the one percent enrollment target is chosen rather than derived
